units.t: The First Peoples of North America

learn: Scientists believe the first people arrived in the Americas at least 15,000 years ago, possibly crossing a land bridge called Beringia or travelling along the coast.
Many Native nations have their own origin stories about how they came to be.
Early cultures like the Mound Builders (Adena, Hopewell and Mississippian) built large earthworks, including Cahokia near present-day St. Louis.
check: The land bridge between Asia and North America is called...
lessons.try: Look at pictures of Cahokia's mounds and describe what life there might have been like.

learn: By 1492, millions of people lived in North America in hundreds of nations.
The Ancestral Puebloans built cliff dwellings like those at Mesa Verde.
The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy united five, later six, nations under the Great Law of Peace.
check: The Haudenosaunee united nations under the...
lessons.try: Compare two Native nations' homes, foods and governments.

learn: Native peoples adapted to every environment, from Arctic coasts to deserts.
Trade networks connected nations across the continent.
Spiritual beliefs often emphasised respect for nature.
lessons.try: Map trade routes between three Native regions.

learn: Europeans explored for the "three Gs": gold, glory and God.
They wanted new trade routes to Asia for spices and silk.
New technology, like the caravel, compass and astrolabe, made long voyages possible.
check: The "three Gs" are gold, glory and...
lessons.try: Write a list of what an explorer might pack for a voyage.

learn: Christopher Columbus sailed for Spain in 1492 and reached the Caribbean.
Ferdinand Magellan's expedition (1519-1522) was the first to sail around the world, though Magellan died on the way.
Jacques Cartier explored the St. Lawrence River for France; Henry Hudson explored for England and the Netherlands.
check: Whose expedition first sailed around the world?
lessons.try: Trace two explorers' routes on a world map.

learn: The Columbian Exchange was the transfer of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and Europe, Africa and Asia.
Corn, potatoes and tomatoes went to Europe. Horses, cattle and wheat came to the Americas.
Diseases like smallpox devastated Native populations.
check: Which went from the Americas to Europe?
Which came to the Americas from Europe?
lessons.try: Make a two-column chart of what went each direction.

learn: The New England colonies were Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Connecticut and Rhode Island.
Pilgrims arrived on the Mayflower in 1620 and signed the Mayflower Compact, an early agreement for self-government.
Rocky soil and cold winters led to fishing, shipbuilding and trade.
check: The Mayflower Compact was an agreement for...
lessons.try: Read the Mayflower Compact and explain it in your own words.

learn: The Middle Colonies were New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Delaware.
Fertile soil made them the "breadbasket colonies", growing wheat and grains.
Pennsylvania, founded by William Penn, welcomed people of many religions.
check: The Middle Colonies were called the...
lessons.try: Describe why the Middle Colonies were called the breadbasket.

learn: The Southern Colonies were Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia.
Warm climate and long growing seasons supported plantations growing tobacco, rice and indigo.
Plantations relied on the forced labour of enslaved Africans.
lessons.try: Compare the economies of the three colonial regions in a chart.

learn: Most colonists were farmers. Families made much of what they needed: candles, soap and clothing.
Towns had craftspeople like blacksmiths, coopers (barrel makers) and printers.
Apprentices learned trades by working for a master for several years.
lessons.try: Research a colonial trade and explain what the worker made.

learn: Enslaved Africans were taken by force across the Atlantic in the Middle Passage, a brutal journey in which many died.
By 1750, enslaved people lived in every colony, though most were in the South.
Enslaved people resisted by preserving culture, working slowly, escaping, and sometimes revolting, as in the Stono Rebellion of 1739.
check: The forced journey across the Atlantic was the...
lessons.try: Read a primary source by Olaudah Equiano and write about his experience.

learn: Colonies had elected assemblies, like Virginia's House of Burgesses (1619), the first in the colonies.
Town meetings in New England let citizens make local decisions.
Britain's king and Parliament still held ultimate power.
check: The first elected assembly in the colonies was...
lessons.try: Hold a mock town meeting about a local issue.

learn: The French and Indian War (1754-1763) was fought between Britain and France, with Native allies on both sides.
Britain won but was left with huge debts.
To pay debts, Britain began taxing the colonies.
check: The French and Indian War was fought between Britain and...
Britain tried to pay debts by...
lessons.try: Make a cause-and-effect chain from the war to new taxes.

learn: The Stamp Act (1765) taxed printed papers. Colonists protested "No taxation without representation."
The Boston Massacre (1770) killed five colonists in a clash with British soldiers.
At the Boston Tea Party (1773), colonists dumped British tea into Boston Harbor.
check: "No taxation without representation" was a protest against...
The Boston Tea Party was in...
lessons.try: Write a protest slogan a colonist might use.

learn: The First Continental Congress met in 1774 to respond to British laws.
Fighting began at Lexington and Concord in April 1775.
Thomas Paine's pamphlet "Common Sense" (1776) argued for independence.
check: The First Continental Congress met in...
lessons.try: Read a passage from "Common Sense" and summarise its argument.

learn: The Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776.
Thomas Jefferson was its main author.
It declares that all men are created equal with rights to "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness", ideals the nation would struggle to extend to everyone.
check: Who was the main author of the Declaration?
It names rights to Life, Liberty and...
lessons.try: Rewrite the Declaration's famous line in your own words.

learn: George Washington led the Continental Army.
The Battle of Saratoga (1777) was a turning point; it convinced France to join the Americans.
The British surrendered at Yorktown in 1781.
check: Which battle convinced France to help?
lessons.try: Make a timeline of five major events of the Revolution.

learn: Women like Abigail Adams wrote about rights; Mercy Otis Warren wrote plays and histories.
About 5,000 African Americans fought for the Patriots; others joined the British, who promised freedom.
The Treaty of Paris (1783) officially ended the war and recognised American independence.
check: Who wrote to her husband to "remember the ladies"?
The Treaty of Paris was signed in...
About how many African Americans fought for the Patriots?
lessons.try: Research one lesser-known person from the Revolution.

learn: The first U.S. government was under the Articles of Confederation.
It created a weak national government that couldn't tax or create an army easily.
Shays' Rebellion (1786-1787) showed the need for a stronger government.
check: Under the Articles, the national government was...
Which rebellion showed the need for change?
lessons.try: List three weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation.

learn: In 1787, delegates met in Philadelphia to write a new constitution.
The Great Compromise created a Senate (equal votes per state) and a House of Representatives (based on population).
The Three-Fifths Compromise counted enslaved people as three-fifths of a person for representation, an unjust compromise.
lessons.try: Debate: should states have equal votes or votes by population?

lessons.t: Three Branches and Checks and Balances
learn: The Constitution created three branches: legislative (Congress), executive (President) and judicial (Supreme Court).
Checks and balances let each branch limit the others.
The president can veto laws; Congress can override with a two-thirds vote; courts can rule laws unconstitutional.
check: The judicial branch is led by the...
Congress can override a veto with a...
lessons.try: Draw a diagram showing checks and balances.

units.t: The Bill of Rights and Citizenship

learn: The Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791.
The First Amendment protects speech, religion, press, assembly and petition.
Other amendments protect the right to a fair trial and protection from unreasonable searches.
check: The Bill of Rights was ratified in...
Which amendment area protects against unreasonable searches?
lessons.try: Make a poster of five Bill of Rights protections.

learn: Later amendments expanded rights: the 13th abolished slavery (1865), the 19th gave women the vote (1920).
The 15th Amendment (1870) said voting couldn't be denied because of race, though unfair laws often blocked Black voters for decades.
The 26th Amendment (1971) lowered the voting age to 18.
lessons.try: Make a timeline of amendments that expanded voting rights.

learn: Citizens have rights and responsibilities.
Responsibilities include obeying laws, paying taxes, serving on juries and voting.
People become citizens by birth in the U.S. or through naturalisation.
check: Becoming a citizen through a legal process is...
lessons.try: Interview someone about why voting matters to them.

lessons.t: Louisiana Purchase and Lewis and Clark
learn: In 1803, Thomas Jefferson bought the Louisiana Territory from France for $15 million.
Lewis and Clark's Corps of Discovery explored it from 1804 to 1806, aided by Sacagawea.
They mapped the land and recorded plants, animals and Native nations.
lessons.try: Read an excerpt from Lewis and Clark's journals.

learn: Manifest Destiny was the belief that the U.S. should expand across the continent.
Settlers travelled the Oregon Trail; the California Gold Rush (1849) brought thousands west.
Expansion came at great cost to Native nations, whose lands were taken.
check: The belief the U.S. should expand across the continent was...
The California Gold Rush began in...
Expansion came at great cost to...
lessons.try: Write a diary entry as a traveller on the Oregon Trail.

learn: The Indian Removal Act (1830) forced Native nations from their homelands in the Southeast.
In 1838-1839, the Cherokee were forced to march west on the Trail of Tears; thousands died.
The Cherokee had their own written language, created by Sequoyah, and a newspaper.
check: The Indian Removal Act was passed in...
The forced march of the Cherokee is called the...
Who created a Cherokee written language?
lessons.try: Learn about Sequoyah's syllabary and why it was important.

units.t: Slavery, the Civil War and Reconstruction

learn: By 1860, about four million people were enslaved in the United States.
Abolitionists like Frederick Douglass and Harriet Tubman worked to end slavery.
The Underground Railroad was a network of secret routes and safe houses helping people escape to freedom.
check: About how many people were enslaved by 1860?
Who escaped slavery and became a famous speaker and writer?
lessons.try: Read a passage from Frederick Douglass's autobiography.

learn: The Civil War (1861-1865) was fought between the Union (North) and the Confederacy (South), mainly over slavery.
President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863.
The war ended in 1865 when General Lee surrendered to General Grant at Appomattox.
check: The Civil War was mainly over...
lessons.try: Read the Gettysburg Address and explain its main idea.

learn: Reconstruction (1865-1877) was the period of rebuilding the South and bringing it back into the Union.
The 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments ended slavery, granted citizenship and protected voting rights.
After Reconstruction, unfair "Jim Crow" laws took away many rights from Black Americans for decades.
check: Took away rights from Black Americans
lessons.try: Make a chart of the three Reconstruction Amendments.
